cards.question: What is a SART (Search and Rescue Transponder)?
options: A device that responds to a 9 GHz radar signal and marks your position on nearby radar screens
A float-free beacon that sends your GPS position to satellites on 406 MHz
A handheld VHF radio that works only on channel 16
cards.explanation: A SART is a radar transponder. When it is triggered by a 9 GHz (X-band) radar, it replies with a signal that appears on the radar display and points rescuers toward your location.

cards.question: How does an activated SART appear on a ship's radar screen?
options: As a line of twelve equally spaced blips running outward from your position along the bearing
As a flashing red circle around the whole screen
As a written text message showing your coordinates
cards.explanation: An activated SART shows a series of 12 equally spaced blips on the radar, starting at the SART and extending outward along the bearing. As the rescuer closes in, the blips widen into arcs.

cards.question: What does an EPIRB transmit when it is activated?
options: A 406 MHz distress alert with your identity and position to the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system
A 9 GHz radar echo to nearby vessels
A spoken voice message on VHF channel 16
cards.explanation: An EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) transmits a coded 406 MHz distress alert, including its beacon ID and GPS position, to search-and-rescue satellites.

cards.question: A helicopter lowers a line to your boat. What must you do first before handling it?
options: Let the line or strop touch the water or the deck first to discharge static electricity
Grab it immediately and make it fast to a cleat
Tie it to the mast so the helicopter can winch the whole boat
cards.explanation: A helicopter builds up a large static charge. Always let the winch wire, hi-line or strop touch the sea or the deck before you handle it, otherwise you can receive an electric shock.

cards.question: While being winched by a helicopter, what must you NEVER do with the winch wire?
options: Make it fast (secure it) to any part of the boat
Let it earth itself in the water before touching it
Follow the instructions given by the winch operator
cards.explanation: Never secure the helicopter's winch wire to the vessel. If the boat moves or rolls, a made-fast wire could drag the helicopter down. Keep the wire free to run at all times.

cards.question: How should you treat a conscious crew member suffering from hypothermia?
options: Handle them gently, move them to shelter, remove wet clothing, insulate and rewarm the core gradually, and give warm sweet drinks
Rub their arms and legs vigorously and give them alcohol to warm up
Put them straight into a very hot bath and make them exercise
cards.explanation: Handle a hypothermia casualty gently, because rough handling can trigger cardiac arrest. Remove wet clothes, insulate them and rewarm the core slowly. Avoid rubbing the limbs, alcohol and sudden intense heat.

cards.question: What is the correct immediate action the moment someone falls overboard?
options: Shout 'Man overboard', throw a lifebuoy, post a dedicated spotter to point at the person, and press the MOB button on the GPS
Go below to call a friend before doing anything on deck
Immediately drop all sails and start preparing a hot drink
cards.explanation: Raise the alarm, throw buoyancy at once, keep a dedicated lookout pointing continuously at the casualty, and mark the position (MOB button, or note the time and course).

cards.question: Why should a hypothermic man-overboard casualty be recovered horizontally where possible?
options: A sudden vertical lift can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure and cardiac arrest (post-rescue collapse)
It simply makes the person easier to photograph
Horizontal recovery is always faster in every situation
cards.explanation: After prolonged immersion, lifting a casualty vertically can trigger circulatory collapse. Recover them as horizontally as practicable and keep them lying down afterwards.

cards.question: What is the correct sequence when launching a liferaft?
options: Check the painter is secured to a strong point, throw the raft overboard, then pull the painter hard to inflate it
Throw the raft over the side still packed and jump in after it
Inflate it on deck first, then lift it into the water
cards.explanation: Make sure the painter (operating line) is tied to a strong point on the boat, launch the canister to leeward, then give the painter a sharp pull to fire the gas bottle and inflate the raft.

cards.question: You have boarded the liferaft. What are the priority actions (remembered as 'cut, stream, close, maintain')?
options: Cut the painter once everyone is aboard and the vessel is clearly lost, stream the drogue, close the canopy, and maintain the raft
Immediately paddle away from the scene as fast as possible
Throw away the knife and the bailer to save weight
cards.explanation: Once all survivors are aboard: Cut the painter (only after the parent vessel is clearly sinking), Stream the sea-anchor/drogue for stability, Close the canopy to retain warmth, and Maintain the raft (bail, first aid, keep a lookout).

cards.question: When should you inflate a lifejacket if you must abandon ship into the water?
options: Once you are clear of the vessel and outside, not while still inside the cabin
Always inflate it fully before leaving your bunk below deck
Never inflate it, because it works better deflated
cards.explanation: An inflated lifejacket makes it very hard to escape through a hatch or doorway and can trap you inside a flooding cabin. Inflate it only once you are clear of the vessel.

cards.question: What is the correct use of a red parachute flare versus a red hand-held flare?
options: A red parachute flare raises the alarm over long distances; a red hand-held flare pinpoints your position to rescuers who are already nearby
Both are only for celebrating at night and carry no distress meaning
The parachute flare is for close range and the hand-held is for long range
cards.explanation: Red parachute (rocket) flares climb high and are seen at long range to alert others. Red hand-held flares guide rescuers onto your exact position once they are close. Orange smoke is the daytime equivalent for pinpointing.
